Determine whether this mapping is one-one, many-one or one-many.
x x3   x
a) one-one
b) many-one
c) one-many
My answer
Dyna Thinking Coach
Echo
say it in your own words
Say it simply: “Every real x is cubed.” The question is whether two different numbers can have the same cube.
Roots
ask why it works
Ask why x2 let two inputs meet: the minus sign disappeared. Work out (−2)3 and 23. Does the sign survive cubing?
YOUR TURN
Use what you found about the sign. Sketch the curve if you need to, then decide.
4
Determine whether this mapping is one-one, many-one or one-many.
x 2x   x
a) one-one
b) many-one
c) one-many
My answer
Dyna Thinking Coach
Translator
turn words into numbers, pictures or steps
Plot a few points: x = −1, 0, 1, 2 give ½, 1, 2, 4. Join them into a curve.
Roots
ask why it works
Ask why the curve has its shape: each step to the right doubles the output. Can the output ever come back down to a value it had earlier?
YOUR TURN
Draw one horizontal line on your sketch. Count the crossings, then name the mapping.
5
Determine whether this mapping is one-one, many-one or one-many.
x 1x   x , x > 0
a) one-one
b) many-one
c) one-many
My answer
Dyna Thinking Coach
Vault
pick what you already know
Recall what the domain says: only x > 0 is allowed. Negative inputs are not part of this mapping at all.
Translator
turn words into numbers, pictures or steps
Make a table for x = ½, 1, 2, 4. As x grows, what happens to the output? Can it come back to a value it had before?
YOUR TURN
Decide if two allowed inputs can share an output.
